MINUTES
  MALIBU PLANNING COMMISSION
  REGULAR MEETING
  NOVEMBER 30, 2023
  COUNCIL CHAMBERS AND TELECONFERENCED
  6:30 P.M.

The following meeting was held in a hybrid format that allowed members of the public to
participate in-person and remotely via Zoom.

CALL TO ORDER

  Chair Peak called the meeting to order at 6:33 p.m.

ROLL CALL

  The following persons were recorded in attendance by the Recording Secretary:

ITEM 2.B.  COMMISSION I STAFF COMMENTS

  Commissioner Smith announced his granddaughter Drew Violet had just celebrated
  her eighth birthday the day after Thanksgiving and his oldest grandson Dylan would
  turn thirteen the next day.

  Vice Chair Mazza wished Dylan a happy birthday and announced he had attended
  the presentation by the City of the sea rise study but felt the study while thorough
  would require adjustments for Planning Commission use. The study covered 75
  rather than 1 00 years and did not consider wave uprush. The Planning Commission
  would require more information than provided before the study should be adopted
  to inform City policy. The study also failed to include Federal Emergency
  Management Agency (FEMA) maps, which impact owners’ ability to obtain
  insurance.

  Commissioner Leonard indicated he would withhold comment in the interests of
  time.

  Due to the essence of time, Commissioner Peak wished everyone well during the
  upcoming holidays.

  Chair Hill noted he would like to reopen the discussion on a potential change to the
  start and end times of Planning Commission meetings to be discussed when Item
  No. 8.A. was heard. He asked for Planning Director Mollica to respond to the letter
  from a member of the public which questioned the composition and practices of the
  Environmental Review Board. He noted as pointed out by Don Schmitz in the sea
  level rise presentation, other agencies such as the California Coastal Commission,
  FEMA, Southern Califomia Edison and Los Angeles County Waterworks were all
  working on their own assessments of sea rise. He questioned what value added the
  City could bring to the discussion. Though the conversation regarded vulnerability,
  there was no discussion of the relative costs or economic factors. The City
  should be mindful of what the incentives were in regard to preservation vs.
  development, and one way (among many) to address that would be to
  look at financial mechanisms such as taxes. Imposition of a coastal
  preservation tax of 1 5 percent on sales of beachfront homes could create a fund
  for compensation for condemned properties. He also suggested a fifteen-year
  limit for mortgages for beachfront homes. Chair Hill noted Councilmember
  Stewart had stated each Councilmember should have his or her representative
  present to deliberate on Planning Commission items. He hoped this was a
  misstatement as Commissioners functioned independently iii a quasi-judicial
  role. Disclosures should include any discussions held on matters with the
  appointing Counci lmember.

  Vice Chair Mazza noted the Planning Commission looked at coastal vulnerability
   Malibu Planning Commission
  Minutes ofNovember 30. 2023
  Page 4 of 10

  as each proposed development came before them. Current State law provided that
  the State became owner of the property if breached by wave uprush.

  Commissioner Peak noted that it was outside the purview of the Planning
  Commission to determine or assess fees or to conduct or fund surveys.

  In response to Chair Hill, Planning Director Mollica explained that the
  Environmental Review Board was an advisory Board rather than a Brown Act Body
  and scheduling of meetings was project driven on an as-needed basis.
  Boardrnernbers reviewed proposed development for both direct and cumulative
  potential impacts on sensitive resources and provided recommendations. A number
  of new members were appointed in 2023 due to attrition and the publicly noticed
  application and interview process was widely publicized. Appointees represented a
  variety of professional fields. Meetings have been held on Zoom and were open to
  the public with recommendations documented and incorporated in agenda reports.

  The Planning Director also provided an update on the winter holiday City Hall
  closure, December 22, 2023 through January 1. 2024. Services available via email
  and phone included Code Enforcement, Building Safety Inspections, Fire Rebuild
  Contract Planner and contract City reviewers. Services unavailable during the
  closure included communication with City staff, Building Safety and Planning
  Online Portals, the public counter, payment processing, and both Planning and
  Building Safety Hotlines (phone and email). He noted that the Malibu Municipal
  Code prohibited any construction on City holidays, which included Christmas and
  New Year’s Day. The update would be publicized via social media, at Planning
  Commission and City Council meetings and via outreach to applicants and owners
  of active projects.
